newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel offers backing to Serbia opposition leader.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel offers backing to Serbia opposition leader.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel gave high-profile backing to Serbia's opposition on Sunday by meeting one of its leaders and warning President Slobodan Milosevic to expect no let-up in international pressure on his authoritarian government.

"The international community has means at its disposal to exercise pressure," Kinkel said after meeting Zoran Djindjic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) alliance. "It appears this pressure is necessary."
But he added full-scale sanctions should not be considered at the moment as they would only harm the population at large.

Djindjic, whose group is campaigning for the recognition of opposition victories in local elections last November, vowed Zajedno would stick to peaceful methods of protest although it did not expect Milosevic to meet its demands.
"We think the crisis will escalate," said Djindjic, who also warned Zajedno could not be held responsible for the actions of individuals if the government resorted to force.

"We will demonstrate peacefully. We've shown in the last two months that we can stick to that," he said. "As for the other side, we can't take responsibility. We don't rule out the use of force by the government."

Djindjic, whose fluent German means he frequently appears in television reports here, said the opposition may have to resort to new forms of peaceful protest, such as large-scale strikes or bringing traffic to a standstill across the country.

Zajedno has sustained daily protests in Belgrade for the last two months. But the number of demonstrators has declined of late to around 30,000 -- well down on the 100,000 seen regularly at the height of the rallies.
Djindjic said his movement could keep up the protests for as long as required.

"There's a critical mass of about 20,000 which is always there," he said. "The important thing is the continuity... it's clear the number of people can't influence the government, only the fact that they're there every day."

Kinkel called on Milosevic to end censorship of the media and to grant autonomy to the province of Kosovo, which is populated mainly by ethnic Albanians. Germany has thousands of asylum-seekers from Kosovo, Kinkel said.
Djindjic faced some tough questions from reporters on his links to former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, who has been indicted on war crimes charges.
He insisted contact with the Bosnian Serbs was necessary to ensure stability in Serbia itself and that he had had contacts with Karadzic because he was Bosnian Serb leader.
"I have contact with political structures not with individual people. They're not important to me," he said. "Karadzic is no longer in office. I've had no contact with him for two years."
